questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I had been to Prague once before a long time ago, and remembered it as being a great place. I liked the idea of riding old trams. The broad selections of courses available at Charles university was also crucial to my decision. During my research I had been disappointed to see that the courses generally available to Erasmus students at KU's partner universities seemed less inspiring than the ones i could choose if i had stayed home - This was not the case at all at CU! here they had courses in fields I had never even heard about, and many interesting formats.

It was also nice that Prague is generally regarded as an affordable city

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, I got tons of mails

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had an extremely thorough orientation week. The Erasmus coordinator and three student ambassadors were with us every step of the way, and they even took us to get our isic cards made and took us to an insurance agency to register our european health insurance. They gave us information about everything from academics and bureaucracy to cool hangout spots and public transportation. They also organized presentations from spokespeople for different Erasmus interest organizations, where we got told about different opportunities. It was almost a little bit much, but it was also pretty comforting because even if you spaced out for a while you felt sure that you didn't miss anything. It also gave me and the other Erasmus students the opportunity to get to know one another before classes started.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I had to write a ton of messages to people on facebook, and i was getting a little panicky at the end, but it worked out beautifully. I loved living with roommates, they made my experience a thousand times better

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I think it's the best way to experience the city, since the dorms are a little isolated. I could very easily go to nearby cafes, markets and spontaneous meetups, while the dormitory students had to travel some more 

I lived in a great apartment with great crazy people, so i never felt alone, but i think that when you live off campus, you miss you on some of the connections with the other Erasmus students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think it's a bit of a rat race in Prague. Housing is very expensive compared to food prices and the average salary of people here, so it isn't easy, and people are desperate, but housing is also hell in Copenhagen, so i wasn't that shocked.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The IT system is crazy old and crazy confusing, but the faculty knows this, and has developed several guides for how to use it, and set up Q&A sessions and all sorts of things, so I was pretty well prepared. It's all about being fast. The registration at the different faculties opnes up at different times and dates and you have to be ready at these times to quickly register for your courses, since its first come first serve. However, if you don't get your courses the first time around, there is no need to panic. Since it's so chaotic, many students register for way more courses than they need, just to be on the safe side, and then they drop the ones that didn't end up appealing to them in the following "add and drop" period.

Many of the faculties operate with a waitlisting system, where you get moved up on the waitlist, as other students drop the course, and often your odds of getting the course are pretty good.

The faculty also recommended us to show up to class in the courses that we didn't get into yet, to check it out, and if we were very interested, they encouraged us to talk to the teacher to see whether or not they could make an exception for us

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always write to Lenka the Erasmus Coordinator, but i didn't need to

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: very successful

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It's all going to work out, even though it helps if you are fast

questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
They weren't very hard. 
sometimes this meant that i could freely immerse myself in the class without stressing out about passing or failing, and sometimes that meant that i was a little bored and spaced out because I didn't really feel stimulated. it really depended on the coursse

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: it really differed from course to course. It seems to me that Charles university has looser rules for how courses can be structured and taught, and the teacher's really made it their own

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really recommend Iranian Cinema: New Borders (course code: ABV100232) and Medieval Origins of Literature Written By and For Women (course code: YBEC205). The teachers were passionate and kind, and the subject matter was both extremely interesting and communicated in a good way. I attended and paid attention in the classes, not to pass, but for my own sake.

Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't participate in any club activities, but there seemed to be some available

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: in our introduction week, we were introduced to the school newspaper, where we were prompted to send in out own contributions, and at the end of my semester i took a course with some local students who invited me to join a workshop for their sound collective club (Sonic Lumina), an initiative i hadn't hear about before. There were also always loads of flyers and posters with events on them in the cafeteria

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: i didn't participate

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I didn't go to that many of the tourist attractions, but i really enjoyed the large hill between Zizkov and Karlin, both the hill itself and the free museum on top of it. 

Another thing i really enjoyed was the many and beautiful cinemas around Prague - many of which also served as cultural hubs that hosted events and things. The cinemas Bio Aero and Bio Oko had a concept called "Blind dates", where you went into the theater with no idea aboout what movie you were about to see, and then afterwards you payed what you thought the experience was worth. It was really fun and a great icebreaker when talking to new people

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: pretty easy. Like Danes, Czechs also have a reputation of being rude (while they are both actually not), so it wasn't that different. Though i think Czechs are generally less performative than Danes, both in their way of dressing and in their way acting, so you are more likely to get blunt service in the Czech Republic.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I didn't get much opportunity to do so, until the very last week or so, and then it felt a little bit too late :(

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It wasn't that challenging

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The cafe/bar culture!! people go to cafe's all the time; alone, with friends, with dogs, with family, and it's really affordable and pleasant. The waiters always come to your table to get your order, and they look at you a bit weirdly if you walk up to the counter, but it doesn't seem fancy, it's very casual for them. The alcohol culture also made an impression on me, in the way that Czech people drink beer all the time, but in a very mundane and civilized way. It's not abnormal to see a person at a cafe 11:00 AM, working on their laptop and enjoying a huge draft beer. Beer doesn't seem to be as much about getting drunk than it is about the taste and feeling of having a beer. The beers are also amazingly good.

questions.answer: take it easy, it's all going to work out

figuring out how easy it actually is to build a new life

drawing a lot 

being alone with my thoughts (and winning)
